idiom_name: translation unit as the grant boundary: file-scope static implementation behind an opaque struct plus a narrow public header
implementation_notes: C has no access control inside a translation unit; the only compiler-enforced knob is linkage, and a file-scope static function or object has internal linkage, so it is reachable from every function in that translation unit and from none outside it (cppreference, storage-class specifiers). The classic structure therefore degenerates into the file: keep the implementation in the .c file as static functions over an opaque struct, publish only the narrow granted operation in the header, and let the helper be another static function in the same file. The hand-built attorney is still justified when the implementation must be visible to exactly one helper and to nothing else in the module - C cannot express that - so the code is organised so that the grant coincides with the translation unit and the boundary is defended by the header plus review rather than by the compiler.
pitfalls: static is a linkage property, not a capability: every function compiled into the same file - including ones added later - gets the whole implementation, so the grant is file-granular and cannot be narrowed to a single helper.

Putting the implementation in a shared header (non-static, or a static inline body) leaks it into every translation unit that includes the header, and a static inline implementation in a header gives every unit its own copy of any state.
const is not privacy: a file-scope const object that is not extern still has external linkage in C (unlike C++), so it stays visible and linkable from other translation units.
